summary: Nigeria moved its short-visit visas fully online in May 2025: most nationalities now apply for an e-Visa (tourism or business) that is normally decided within about 48 hours, replacing the old visa-on-arrival scheme, while ECOWAS citizens continue to enter freely under the bloc's free-movement protocol.

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months on arrival, with at least one blank page for the entry stamp.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required when arriving from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission; as Nigeria itself is a yellow-fever country, vaccination is recommended for all visitors and the yellow card is often asked for regardless of routing.

travelInsurance.text: Not a condition of entry, but strongly recommended — private healthcare in Lagos and Abuja is decent but expensive, and serious cases may need evacuation.

onwardTicket.text: A return or onward ticket is part of the e-Visa application and is checked by airlines before boarding.

source.name: Nigeria Immigration Service — official e-Visa portal

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published for short visits; e-Visa applications may ask for evidence of means or a host's details.

declarations.name: Digital Landing and Exit Card
declarations.submitWindow: Before arrival in / departure from Nigeria
declarations.text: Since May 2025 all non-Nigerian travelers must complete a free digital Landing Card before arrival and an Exit Card before departure, through the Nigeria Immigration Service online portal — airlines check the QR confirmation at check-in.

currencyLimits.text: Cash above USD 10,000 (or the equivalent in any currency) must be declared on arrival and departure.

notes: Narcotics offenses carry severe penalties; some prescription medicines (e.g. Strong painkillers) need supporting paperwork.
Export of antiquities and wildlife products is prohibited without a permit.

payments.text: POS card payments and bank-transfer apps are everywhere in Lagos and Abuja, though foreign cards can be declined. Carry naira cash as a fallback and change money only at banks or licensed bureaux de change.

safety.text: Risk varies sharply by state: Lagos, Abuja and much of the south-west are visited routinely with sensible precautions, while the north-east and north-west and some Middle Belt and riverine states are do-not-travel zones due to terrorism, banditry and kidnapping. Plan state by state against current advisories.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Nigeria Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: November to February is the dry season — cooler, with passable roads and the Harmattan haze; the June–September rains bring flooding, especially in the south.

idp.text: Nigeria is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: Nigeria is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Nigeria yet.

tips.text: Apply only at evisa.immigration.gov.ng — lookalike "Nigeria visa" sites charging inflated fees are common. The Nigeria Immigration Service lists the official portal on immigration.gov.ng.
Check advisories for each state on your route, not the country rating: the gap between Lagos and, say, Borno or Zamfara is enormous. Avoid road travel between cities after dark anywhere.
Complete the free digital Landing Card before you fly and the Exit Card before you leave — airlines ask for the confirmation at check-in and paper forms are no longer used.
Change money only at banks or licensed bureaux and keep transfer apps in mind — street changers and inflated "parallel" rates invite scams and counterfeit notes.
Carry your yellow fever certificate — port health officers frequently check it on arrival, especially if you have transited another African country.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Nigeria?
faq.answer: Most travelers do. Since May 2025 short tourist and business visits are handled through Nigeria's official e-Visa, open to some 170+ nationalities including the US, UK, Canada and the EU, with decisions normally within 48 hours. ECOWAS citizens enter without a visa under the bloc's free-movement protocol, and a small number of nationalities must still apply at a Nigerian embassy.

faq.question: Does Nigeria still issue visas on arrival?
faq.answer: No. The visa-on-arrival scheme was discontinued when the e-Visa launched on May 1, 2025. You must be approved online before boarding. Previously issued VOA approvals expired at the end of May 2025.

faq.question: How long does the Nigeria e-Visa take?
faq.answer: Most correctly submitted applications are decided within 24–48 hours, and the approval arrives by email. Apply a week or so ahead in case additional checks are needed.

faq.question: Can US citizens get a Nigeria e-Visa?
faq.answer: Yes — US passport holders are eligible for the e-Visa for tourism or business, applying online at evisa.immigration.gov.ng. Fees follow Nigeria's reciprocity schedule, so the US tariff is at the higher end.

faq.question: Is yellow fever vaccination required for Nigeria?
faq.answer: Formally it is required if you arrive from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission, but Nigeria is itself a yellow-fever-risk country — vaccination is recommended for all visitors and the certificate is often checked on arrival.

faq.question: What is the Nigeria Landing Card?
faq.answer: A free digital arrival/departure declaration introduced with the e-Visa in May 2025. Every non-Nigerian traveler completes the Landing Card online before arrival and an Exit Card before departure; airlines check the confirmation code at check-in.
